summary:
InfoFlame is an interactive dashboard built on combustion experiment data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system. It helps answer how fire behaves in different environments.

Users describe a mission environment by setting the oxygen level, pressure, airflow and gravity. InfoFlame then ranks and summarizes the NASA investigations most relevant to that environment, compares them side by side and shows where no experiment has been done yet. It visualizes how easily materials burn in space, how much suppressant gas is needed to put a fire out and whether smoke detectors can see the smoke. It then turns these results into clear design takeaways for preventing, detecting and suppressing fires.

An AI assistant answers questions in plain language, using only the project’s data and citing its sources.

Engineers can use InfoFlame to check a cabin design against real test results, researchers can download the cleaned data, and students can see why a flame in orbit behaves differently from one on Earth.

View our repository

GitHub link: https://github.com/mari4kaa/spacecrammers-2026

What does InfoFlame do?

Using InfoFlame, users can:

  • Set a mission scenario: choose a preset (ISS, lunar base, exploration atmosphere, Mars habitat, spacesuit, oxygen-enriched room on Earth) or set the oxygen, pressure, air speed and gravity themselves.
  • Find and read the relevant research: see the 24 PSI combustion investigations ranked for that scenario, with a plain-language summary, key findings and sources for each.
  • Compare investigations: put up to four side by side and see what they share, how they differ and which ones used the same flight hardware.
  • See where the data stops: check which conditions no experiment has covered yet, from partial gravity to low pressure.
  • Check flammability: see the lowest oxygen at which a material keeps burning in microgravity, compared with Earth.
  • Get design takeaways: read what the data means for fire prevention, detection and suppression in their scenario, backed by measured flight results.
  • Ask the data: ask questions in plain language and get answers with checked citations.
  • Download the data: export the cleaned test data, the data-quality log and every investigation summary.

Features

Mission scenario and ranking

Everything starts with the mission scenario at the top of the page. As the user moves the oxygen, pressure, air speed and gravity controls, InfoFlame shows the oxygen partial pressure and flags conditions no PSI test reached. It then re-ranks all 24 investigations. Each score (0-100) is split into colored segments, so users can see why an investigation ranks where it does. The mission map plots every test in the database against the scenario, and the top three design takeaways appear beside the ranking.

Investigation cards

Clicking an investigation opens its card. It starts with two short explanations: one in plain words and one for engineers. Below them are the test conditions, objective, fuel and sample size, sensors and hardware. Key findings each name their source report, and a "Relevance to your habitat" section is recomputed for the current scenario. Links lead to the original PSI page and DOI.

Compare and hardware families

Users can pick up to four investigations. InfoFlame automatically writes what they share (overlapping oxygen and pressure ranges, common measurements) and how they differ (hardware, fuel phase, variables).

A row-by-row table compares objectives, conditions, sensors and headline results. Hardware families group the investigations that flew on the same equipment, with NASA photos, so users know which results are directly comparable

Gaps and partial gravity

The Gaps tab counts how many tests ran near the scenario for each fuel type, and states plainly what is missing. An "Atmospheres from Earth to spacesuit" chart places Earth, the ISS, a lunar base, the exploration atmosphere and a spacesuit on one oxygen-pressure map, together with every PSI test.

Because PSI has no partial-gravity data yet, a separate panel bounds the Moon and Mars case with microgravity and Earth results, and lists the upcoming experiments (LUCI, FM2, SoFIE) that will fill the gap.

Flammability boundary

This tab turns a figure from the BASS-II report into an interactive model. It shows the lowest oxygen at which a PMMA (acrylic) sample keeps burning as a function of air speed, with confidence and prediction bands. The user's scenario is marked on the chart with a verdict.

The key result: in microgravity PMMA kept burning down to about 13.9% O₂ near 2 cm/s air speed, below the 15.4% limit on Earth. The limits of the model are listed beside it.

Design takeaways and safety evidence

Seven design takeaways translate the data into what it means for equipment and controls: materials, ventilation, small fires in still air, smoke detectors, invisible cool flames, inert-gas suppression and untested conditions. Each one shows a status for the scenario, the tested conditions behind it and its source, and recalculates when the scenario changes.

Below them, three charts show the measured flight data behind the takeaways: which small flames kept burning in still air (83 ISS tests), how far a suppressant must lower the oxygen (FLEX droplets) and how large smoke particles are compared with the ISS smoke detector's limits (SAME).

Ask the data

The AI assistant answers questions about the investigations in plain language or at engineering level. It can only use the dashboard's data through lookup tools and a search over 24 public reports, and it cites investigation IDs, table rows and report pages. The page checks every citation against what the lookups actually returned and labels each answer as AI-generated.

Data and export

The cleaned test matrix (1,958 rows from 19 PSI tables) can be filtered and downloaded as CSV or JSON. Every row keeps its original PSI file and row number.

The data-quality report lists all 157 issues found while cleaning (typos, spreadsheet auto-fill errors, wrong units, duplicates) and what was done with each.

Incidents and Earth benefits

A timeline links real spacecraft fire events (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir, the Artemis II smoke alarm) to the investigations that address them. A second timeline shows NASA fire-safety spinoffs used on Earth, from firefighter air tanks to water-mist extinguishers.

How does InfoFlame work?

  1. Data collection: Python scripts pull the metadata, experiment tables and report files of every combustion investigation from the PSI repository's data service (snapshot of 14 November 2026). Two non-combustion results were excluded, leaving 24 investigations.
  2. Data cleaning: Each PSI table has its own format, so the scripts convert 19 of them into one schema: fuel, sample size, oxygen, pressure, air speed, diluent, outcome and a key measurement. Every value keeps its PSI file and row number, and every fix is written to the data-quality log.
  3. Summaries: The investigation summaries and findings were written with AI assistance from the PSI reports and NASA papers, then fact-checked against the source passages. Each finding names its source.
  4. Ranking: A fixed formula scores each investigation on seven factors: safety focus, closeness to the scenario, material realism, fire scale, gravity relevance, data richness and model-ready numbers. Users can change the weights. The score is computed in the browser, not by AI.
  5. Flammability boundary: We digitized the 49 test points of Figure 6.10 in the BASS-II report and refitted the report's own equation with 3,000 bootstrap resamples to get 90% bands. Our curve stays within 0.33 percentage points of the report's equation.
  6. Safety evidence and takeaways: Measured values were copied from the papers behind the cards: 83 ISS still-air tests (Dehghani & Quintiere 2023), droplet oxygen limits by suppressant gas (Dietrich et al. 2014) and smoke particle sizes (SAME Final Report) against ISS detector limits (Urban et al. 2007). Fixed rules turn them into the seven takeaways for the current scenario.
  7. AI assistant: Questions go to Google Gemini through a small Cloudflare Worker that keeps the API key off the page. Gemini can only answer through nine lookup tools over the same data and a full-text search of 24 public reports (2,636 passages with page numbers). The page then checks each citation against the lookup results.
  8. Hosting: The whole dashboard is one static web page with the data built in, hosted on GitHub Pages. Everything except the assistant works without a server.

Benefits

  • One place for scattered data. Results from 24 investigations, stored in differently formatted tables and long reports, can be searched, compared and downloaded together.
  • Answers for a specific mission. Instead of browsing a database, users start from their own conditions and see what applies to them.
  • Explainable results. Scores show their parts, every number links to its source, and untested conditions are flagged rather than hidden.
  • For different readers. Plain-language and engineering explanations sit side by side, so the same page works for students and specialists.
  • Free and easy to open. No account or installation; it works on phones, tablets and desktops.

Intended impact

Future lunar habitats and rovers are planned with more oxygen and lower pressure than the ISS, and the PSI data show that materials can burn at lower oxygen in microgravity than Earth tests suggest.

InfoFlame helps engineers check materials, ventilation, smoke detectors and suppression systems against real flight results for those conditions. Researchers get a clean, citable dataset and a clear list of what still needs testing, such as partial gravity and low pressure. Students and the public can see why fire behaves differently in space. The same questions also matter on Earth, in oxygen-enriched hospital rooms, hyperbaric chambers and submarines.

What makes it creative

  • Users start from a habitat’s conditions instead of browsing by experiment.
  • It turns a static figure from a NASA report into an interactive flammability model with uncertainty bands.
  • It points out conditions no experiment has reached: partial gravity, pressures below 6.3 psi, solids above 22.2% O₂. For Moon and Mars gravity it gives the range between microgravity and Earth results.
  • Measured ISS results become practical design advice, such as how much inert gas suppression needs at a given oxygen level, each linked to its tests.
  • The AI assistant can only answer from the project's data, and the page checks its citations.

Factors we considered

In what the dashboard shows

  • The whole atmosphere, not just oxygen: Oxygen fraction and oxygen partial pressure are shown together: a lunar cabin at 30% O₂ and 10.2 psi has almost the same partial pressure as Earth air (3.06 vs 3.08 psi) but is far more flammable.
  • Air movement: Air speed is a scenario control, because without buoyancy in microgravity, ventilation decides whether a flame survives.
  • Gravity: Users can choose microgravity, Moon, Mars or Earth. Since no partial-gravity tests exist, the Moon and Mars cases are bounded by microgravity and Earth results and clearly labelled.
  • Fuel type and fire size: Solids, liquid droplets, gases and smoke are shown separately, and the ranking weighs realistic spacecraft materials and larger fires (such as Saffire) above small lab samples.
  • Prevention, detection and suppression: The user's safety focus changes both the ranking and the design takeaways.
  • Measured vs assumed: Values PSI did not record (for example cabin oxygen in some tests) are marked as assumed and can be hidden, and conditions outside the tested range are flagged instead of extrapolated.
  • Uncertainty: The flammability model shows confidence and prediction bands, and its limits are listed next to it.
  • Different readers: Every card has a plain-language and an engineering explanation, and the assistant can answer at either level.

In how we built it

  • Numbers can be traced to a PSI file and row or a report page. We fact-checked all AI-written findings and reviewed the safety evidence against the original papers.
  • AI use is disclosed on the page, in the repository and in the data files, as rules require. Every assistant answer is labelled with the model name.
  • PSI data are CC0 and cited by DOI. From journal papers we use only measured values, with a citation on every row. The photos are NASA images, credited and linked, with no NASA logos.
  • The layout was tested on phone, tablet and desktop.

Tools we used

Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the dashboard; Python for the data pipeline.

Libraries: Plotly.js for charts; Requests, NumPy and SciPy for downloading data, curve fitting and bootstrap statistics; pdftotext (Poppler) for extracting report text.

NASA data: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and its data service; NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) papers; NASA photos.

AI: Google Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash-lite, with gemini-3.1-flash-lite as fallback) for the live assistant. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with writing code, extracting data from reports and drafting summaries. The demo video's voice-over was generated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech, the video was edited with Claude’s assistance. All AI use is disclosed in AI_USE.md, the site’s Method tab covers Claude and Gemini, and the video labels its own voice-over and editing.

Hosting and services: GitHub and GitHub Pages; Cloudflare Workers (Wrangler) for the AI proxy.

Hardware: a laptop; no special hardware.

Future plans

  • Partial gravity: add LUCI, FM2 and SoFIE results as soon as they reach PSI, so the Moon and Mars case is measured rather than bounded.
  • Richer models: extend the flammability boundary to other materials and to lower pressures, and add the SAME-R particle-size spreadsheets.
  • Live data: refresh the dataset automatically when PSI publishes new investigations.
